source.title: Atomic Literary Styling: Mechanistic Manipulation of Prose Generation in Neural Language Models

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses individual neurons as units for activation analysis and intervention, but does not test the claim versions’ neuron-job shares, explanation prediction accuracy, or neuron-based attribution-graph sufficiency.
record.gate_note: The paper reports no counts of neurons with one or multiple jobs and does not test explanations against activations they were not written from. It does report ablations of discriminative neurons and their effects on a literary-style metric; those results are recorded as findings about neurons but do not test any listed version. Cited claims about sparse or interpretable features are not this study’s results.
record.test_reason: The study ranks GPT-2 Medium MLP neurons by how well they separate Melville from GPT-4 imitation text. It then ablates and steers them, scoring the effect with a stylometric metric. It reports no shares of neurons with one job, two jobs or not understood. It does not score explanations against new activations or build attribution graphs. Its manual reading of max-activating contexts for the top 50 neurons is used descriptively and never checked for prediction. The ablation 'causality gap' concerns causal effect on generation, not whether an explanation predicts firing, so it is a related but different construct from V6.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that activation-based discrimination does not establish causal necessity, since ablating discriminative neurons often improved their style metric. They argue interpretability needs causal validation such as ablation, patching and circuit analysis.
record.recipe_differences: Different model and task: GPT-2 Medium literary-style discrimination and ablation, rather than a Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit or held-out scoring of neuron explanations.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that steering effects persist but weaken on out-of-distribution prompts, with 15–20% change instead of 25–30%.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablating neurons that discriminate Melville from GPT-4 imitation text in GPT-2 Medium gives mixed individual effects. Cumulative ablation of up to 50 layer-21 neurons raises the composite style score from 0.793 to 0.997.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neurons selected for discriminating a target style on input text do not reliably cause that style in generation when ablated.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablation across late-layer combinations gives non-monotonic degradation: +3.4%, +11.4%, +1.8% and +20.7%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The effect of ablating style-discriminative neurons depends on which late layers are targeted.

record.problems: The study uses one author and one text, GPT-2 Medium (355M parameters), and a simple composite style metric; it reports that human evaluation is needed. No random-neuron ablation control or uncertainty estimates for the ablation results are stated. The text also reports 27,122 significant neurons at p < 0.05 despite describing a Bonferroni-corrected threshold of approximately 10⁻⁸, and its layer-wise table gives maximum |d| values up to 3.12 while the surrounding results describe the maximum as about 1.4.
record.rows_left_out: Steering-method metric results and robustness results were not extracted: they report effects of style-vector or steering interventions, not neuron-job shares, explanation prediction, or attribution-graph sufficiency. The paper’s neuron ablation results are retained above.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B audit and no shares of neuron poles by number of jobs.
Only GPT-2 Medium is studied, with no interpretable-neuron shares across models or scale.
No vision models, no InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron, no pose analysis.
No comparison of architectures, regularization or tools, and no interpretable-share estimates.
No attribution graphs and no replacement-model comparison.
Max-activating contexts are inspected manually but never tested for predicting activations on other text.
No simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: This is a single-author preprint with several internal inconsistencies. The text says 'p < 0.05' while describing a Bonferroni threshold of about 10⁻⁸. Max |d| is given as 1.4 in the text but up to 3.12 in Tables 1–2. The critical neuron L18N3395 is absent from the top-20 table. The style metric is a simple composite, there is no random-neuron ablation control, and only three prompts are used. None of this affects the verdict, because no version is tested.

versions.untested_parts: Does not audit Qwen3-32B or report shares of neuron poles assigned one job, two jobs, or not understood.
Tests only GPT-2 Medium and does not measure the share of interpretable neurons across models, architectures, or scales.
Does not examine InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons, pose, or recursive generalization.
Does not compare architecture, regularization, or tools, or estimate interpretable-neuron shares in vision models.
Does not build attribution graphs or test whether they explain behavior without a replacement model.
Manually inspects maximally activating contexts but does not test explanations on separate activations or measure whether they predict where neurons fire.
Does not score neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

rows.subject: GPT-2 Medium
rows.operation_detail: Individually zeroed each of the top 10 discriminative neurons during generation and assessed literary-style degradation.
rows.measure: Literary-style degradation; aggregate across individual ablations
rows.value: 4 of 10 neurons showed degradation when removed (up to 32.6% for the most critical neuron); average effect was −8.8% degradation.
rows.note: The reported aggregate is mixed: some individual removals degraded style, while the average effect indicates improvement.
rows.check: Ablation effect on a style metric, not any version's measure. The text names the most critical neuron as L18N3395, which is not in its own top-20 table, so the subject set is internally inconsistent. The 'partial' state has no version to be judged against.
